1-section-504.pdf
Not every student with a disability has an IEP
Not every student with a disability has an IEP.
Many have a Section 504 plan instead: accommodations, but no special education services.
In the typical U.S. school district in 2023–24, about 2.7 of every 100 students had a 504 plan. In Connecticut's typical district, it was 8.1. In Texas, 7.9. In Kansas and New Mexico, 0.6.
That is more than a thirteen-fold gap between states under the same federal law.
A 504 plan can be the right support. It can also reflect a school's habits about when to refer a student for an IEP evaluation. The numbers alone cannot tell you which.
If your child has a 504 plan, it is fair to ask whether an IEP evaluation was ever offered.

Wed, Jan 6
Who is an IEP written for?
On paper, the child. In many schools, the document is also written for an auditor.

The draft is often finished before the family walks in, in software built around required fields. Goals are measurable because the monitoring checklist asks for measurable goals. Services are listed in minutes because minutes can be counted.
None of that is wrong on its own. But a document built to pass review is not the same as a plan for how a child will spend tomorrow.
One test: could a substitute teacher read the IEP and know what to do differently for this student by 9 a.m.?

How do students with IEPs leave high school?
How do students with IEPs leave high school?
Among districts with reported data, the typical U.S. district in 2023–24 saw about 78.9 of every 100 students with IEPs who left school leave with a regular diploma.
In New Jersey's typical district, it was 96.0. In Wisconsin, 93.5. In South Carolina, 58.5. In Texas, 48.5.
State rules shape these numbers: what counts as a regular diploma, which other certificates a state offers, and when a student is counted as leaving.
A diploma rate is a starting question for a district, not a ranking of states.
You can look up your own district in the IDEA Atlas.

When critical scholars say special education has become about compliance, what do we mean?

Thomas Skrtic argued decades ago that schools are organized as bureaucracies. They run on standard routines. Students who do not fit the routines get sorted into a separate system, and that system gets routines of its own: timelines, forms, signatures.
Compliance is what those routines look like from the outside. A file can be complete and on time while nothing changes in the classroom.
That is not a reason to ignore the law. The law is what gives families standing. It is a reason to ask, every time, what the paperwork changed for the student.

Most of the day outside a general class
How many students with IEPs spend most of the school day outside a general class?
In the typical U.S. district in 2024–25, about 7.1 of every 100 school-age students with IEPs were in a general class less than 40% of the day.
In New York's typical district, it was 16.0. In South Carolina, 14.9. In Georgia, 14.2. In New Jersey, 9.6.

Each of those placements is decided by an IEP team, one student at a time. Taken together, the decisions form patterns that differ sharply from state to state, which raises a question about how much local habit shapes them.
Where does your district fall? Look it up in the IDEA Atlas.

Every state reports how well its schools involve parents of students with IEPs.
The measure is a survey. Parents are asked whether the school helped them take part in their child's education. Nationally, 84.8% said yes in 2024–25.
That number matters, and it is also thin. It cannot tell you whether a parent's idea ended up in the IEP, whether the meeting time worked for the family, or whether anyone asked the student.
Participation is something a family does. Counting it with a checkbox turns it into something a school is graded on.

What do restraint and seclusion zeros mean?
Of the 16,450 U.S. school districts with reported data for 2023–24, 68% reported that no student with an IEP was physically restrained. 87% reported no seclusion.
Another 2,060 districts did not report at all.
Some of those zeros are accurate. Others may reflect what gets written down. Schools count their own restraint and seclusion, and the count depends on the record.
When a district reports zero, the useful question is "how would we know?"
Look up your district's figures in the IDEA Atlas.
